doc.title: Fred Wesley interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 21, 2024

chapter: Studio work and playing by ear
title: James Brown's impossible arranging demands
summary: Brown asked for harp, cello solos and Don't Fence Me In; Wesley made them work, compared by Rowe to George Martin.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: In the arranging you’ve done, if you think back on it, I’m wondering if something, an artist or a situation comes to your mind that was really challenging and that stretched what you had been doing previously, if it’s writing for strings or something like that.

Well the James Brown job was most challenging too because he would — James Brown would just sing stuff off the top of his head but you had to do it. He would say, “Okay use a harp right here.” A harp? What did James Brown want with a harp in his band you know? But he had to have this harp, and he’d say, “Okay we want a cello solo in this part.” A cello solo? Why? I cannot do this. You know? But you’d have to make it work. Had to make it work. And he would say, ah, you see, you didn’t think it would work did you. And he would laugh because he had known, he knew he had challenged me. You know? And he would say, he would tell me to do tunes like “Don’t Fence Me In.” I’d say now why does James Brown want to do a tune like “Don’t Fence Me In”? You know. But the challenge, I came up to the challenge. I wrote an arrangement for it and Warren Bernhardt, he played the clavinet part on it, and it was absolutely beautiful you know. And James Brown was the most challenging musician that I ever worked for because he would say things that were totally ridiculous but you had to make it come out right.

Wow. That is a challenge because people who don’t know about the limitations of instruments or in scoring and all that stuff, but they get these marvelous ideas in their head. Like George Martin with the Beatles.
He would translate some of those ideas they had and make them reality.
So you’re the George Martin of the James Brown — or vice versa. He was the Fred Wesley for the Beatles.
